title: “I am the man that hath seen affliction” — who is the man?
summary: Lamentations 3:1 begins with “I am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath”. The verse does not say who the man is.
text: KJV Lamentations 3:1: “I Am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath.” KJV Lamentations 3:14: “I was a derision to all my people; and their song all the day.” KJV Lamentations 3:48: “Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water for the destruction of the daughter of my people.”
reasoning: Chapter 3 is spoken by “I”, who says “I was a derision to all my people” (3:14) and weeps “for the destruction of the daughter of my people” (3:48). The chapter does not name him or say whether he is one person or speaks for the people. Possible readings, named only as readings: a prophet speaking his own sufferings; a figure who speaks for the whole people; a representative sufferer. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the three verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more about the speaker.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: I Am the man that hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath

title: “The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord, was taken in their pits” — who is the anointed?
summary: Lamentations 4:20 says “the anointed of the Lord” was “taken in their pits”. The verse does not name him or say who “their” refers to.
text: KJV Lamentations 4:19: “Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven: they pursued us upon the mountains, they laid wait for us in the wilderness.” KJV Lamentations 4:20: “The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord, was taken in their pits, of whom we said, Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen.”
reasoning: The verse says the people had said of him, “Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen”, and that he “was taken in their pits”. The verse before it speaks of pursuers who “laid wait for us in the wilderness”. Neither verse names the anointed one or those who took him. Possible readings, named only as readings: the reigning king of Judah; the line of kings as a whole; another person set apart by anointing. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the two verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek (the Greek of this verse is the subject of a separate record), and does not claim that no other passage says more about the anointed one.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: the anointed of the Lord, was taken in their pits

title: “Thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called” — which day, and who are “they”?
summary: Lamentations 1:21 says “thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called, and they shall be like unto me”. The verse does not say which day this is or who “they” are.
text: KJV Lamentations 1:21: “They have heard that I sigh: there is none to comfort me: all mine enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that thou hast done it: thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called, and they shall be like unto me.” KJV Lamentations 1:22: “Let all their wickedness come before thee; and do unto them, as thou hast done unto me for all my transgressions: for my sighs are many, and my heart is faint.”
reasoning: The speaker says the day was “called” and that “they” shall be like the speaker. The verse names “mine enemies” earlier in the same sentence, and the next verse speaks of “all their wickedness”. The two verses do not say on what occasion the day was called, who the Lord is said to have called it against, or what “like unto me” would be. Possible readings, named only as readings: a day of judgment on the nations that rejoiced; the same day of anger the speaker has suffered; a day proclaimed by an earlier prophecy. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the two verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more about the day.
